faq.a: Yes, men can experience galactorrhoea, and it often indicates an underlying hormonal imbalance, such as hyperprolactinaemia, or a pituitary tumour. It requires similar investigation as in women.

No, galactorrhoea can be physiological (e.g., due to stress or nipple stimulation) or drug-induced, which are often reversible. However, it can also signal more serious conditions like pituitary tumours or hypothyroidism, so investigation is always warranted.
faq.q: Is galactorrhoea always a sign of a serious problem?

faq.a: Drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia is a very common cause, particularly from antipsychotics, antidepressants, and certain anti-emetics. Prolactinomas are also common, but less frequent than drug effects.
faq.q: What is the most common cause of galactorrhoea?

exam: A 28-year-old woman presents with bilateral milky nipple discharge and irregular periods. What is your initial diagnostic approach, especially considering a low-resource setting? — First, rule out pregnancy with a urine hCG. Then, take a detailed drug history, including traditional remedies. Perform a physical exam looking for signs of hypothyroidism or pituitary mass (e.g., visual fields). Order serum prolactin and TSH levels. If prolactin is very high, consider empirical tr

You suspect drug-induced galactorrhoea in a patient on antipsychotics. How would you confirm this and what is your management plan? — Confirm by reviewing the medication list and checking serum prolactin. If prolactin is elevated and other causes are ruled out, discuss with the prescribing physician to consider reducing the dose, switching to an alternative drug with less prolactin-elevating effect, or adding a dopamine agonist if necessary and appropriate.

A patient with galactorrhoea has a very high prolactin level (>250 ng/mL) and bitemporal hemianopia on confrontation visual field testing. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate next step? — This strongly suggests a prolactinoma with suprasellar extension compressing the optic chiasm. The immediate next step is urgent referral for neurosurgical or endocrinological evaluation, and if available, an MRI of the pituitary.

How do you differentiate true galactorrhoea from other types of nipple discharge? — True galactorrhoea is milky, typically white or clear, and often bilateral. Other discharges can be bloody (intraductal papilloma, carcinoma), purulent (infection), or serous/greenish (duct ectasia, fibrocystic changes). The key is the milky appearance.

A patient with galactorrhoea has normal prolactin levels. What are some possible explanations? — Possible explanations include physiological causes (excessive nipple stimulation, stress), chest wall irritation, local breast pathology, or idiopathic galactorrhoea. A careful history and physical exam are crucial to identify these non-hyperprolactinaemic causes.

What are the potential complications of untreated hyperprolactinaemia causing galactorrhoea? — In women, complications include menstrual irregularities, infertility, and long-term bone loss (osteoporosis) due to hypoestrogenism. In men, it can cause hypogonadism, erectile dysfunction, and infertility. If due to a prolactinoma, mass effect can lead to headaches and visual field defects.
ai.title: Galactorrhoea: Causes and Clinical Approach
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Galactorrhoea is the inappropriate lactation, unrelated to childbirth or breastfeeding. It results from hormonal imbalances, primarily elevated prolactin, or local breast stimulation. A systematic clinical approach is crucial to identify the underlying cause and guide management.

b: Not all nipple discharge is galactorrhoea; it must be milky.
Can occur in both sexes and at any age.
Often associated with hyperprolactinaemia, but not always.
sections.p: Galactorrhoea is defined as the secretion of milky fluid from the breast in men, or in women who are not pregnant or breastfeeding, or who have not been pregnant or lactating for at least 12 months. It can be unilateral or bilateral, spontaneous or expressed. It is a sign, not a disease, and warrants investigation to identify the underlying cause, which can range from physiological to pathological conditions.

b: TRH (Thyrotropin-releasing hormone) can stimulate prolactin release.
Breast stimulation, stress, and certain medications can increase prolactin.
sections.p: Prolactin is the primary hormone responsible for milk production. Its secretion is tonically inhibited by dopamine from the hypothalamus. Any disruption to this inhibitory pathway or direct stimulation of prolactin-producing cells can lead to hyperprolactinaemia and subsequent galactorrhoea. Understanding the neuroendocrine regulation of prolactin is central to diagnosing the causes.

b: History: onset, duration, associated symptoms (headaches, visual changes, menstrual irregularities, erectile dysfunction, drug use, herbal remedies).
Examination: assess for bilateral/unilateral, spontaneous/expressible discharge, consistency, colour. Look for signs of hypothyroidism (goitre, bradycardia) or pituitary mass (visual field defects).

Causes can be physiological (stress, nipple stimulation), pharmacological (antipsychotics, opioids, metoclopramide), endocrine (prolactinoma, hypothyroidism, PCOS), or local (chest wall irritation, breast surgery).
sections.p: A clinician must differentiate true galactorrhoea from other forms of nipple discharge and systematically investigate its causes, especially in low-resource settings where advanced imaging or hormonal assays may be limited. The approach involves a detailed history, physical examination, and targeted investigations to rule out serious conditions like pituitary tumours or hypothyroidism.

t.b: Rules out pregnancy as a physiological cause of lactation. A positive result indicates pregnancy.
Measures prolactin concentration. Elevated levels (hyperprolactinaemia) suggest a cause like prolactinoma, drug effect, or hypothyroidism. Levels >200 ng/mL strongly suggest a prolactinoma.
Screens for hypothyroidism, which can cause hyperprolactinaemia due to increased TRH. An elevated TSH with low T4 indicates primary hypothyroidism.
Assesses for chronic kidney disease, which can impair prolactin clearance. Elevated creatinine suggests renal impairment.
Evaluates liver disease, which can affect hormone metabolism. Abnormal LFTs may indicate hepatic dysfunction.
Identifies drugs known to cause hyperprolactinaemia (e.g., antipsychotics, metoclopramide, verapamil, opioids). Discontinuation or substitution may resolve galactorrhoea.
Screens for bitemporal hemianopia, a sign of optic chiasm compression by a pituitary tumour. Loss of peripheral vision suggests chiasmal compression. (If formal perimetry is unavailable).

Visualizes pituitary gland to detect adenomas (prolactinomas). Identifies size and location of tumour. (If unavailable, consider empirical treatment for suspected prolactinoma if prolactin is very high and other causes ruled out, or refer to higher centre).

b: Distinguish true galactorrhoea from other nipple discharges (purulent, bloody, serous).
Remember drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia is a very common cause.
Consider hypothyroidism as a reversible cause.
In low-resource settings, a high prolactin level with visual field defects strongly points to a prolactinoma, even without MRI.
sections.p: Examiners will test your ability to systematically approach galactorrhoea, considering common causes first, especially those relevant to the local context. Focus on the diagnostic pathway and management principles, including when to refer.

b: Not taking a comprehensive drug history, including traditional remedies.
Failing to check TSH, especially in women with menstrual irregularities.
Not performing a careful visual field assessment.
Assuming all milky discharge is pathological; physiological causes are common.
Ignoring unilateral galactorrhoea, which can still be due to systemic causes.
sections.p: Students often jump to prolactinoma without considering more common or easily treatable causes. Another mistake is not performing a thorough medication review or overlooking subtle signs of hypothyroidism.

whenToSeekHelp: New visual disturbances (e.g., blurred vision, loss of peripheral vision)
Signs of neurological deficit (e.g., weakness, numbness)
Rapidly increasing breast mass associated with discharge
Discharge that is bloody or purulent
